passage:
Friday
I finally told Pankaj Sir. I'm taking commerce, not science. He has been giving me extra physics problems since Class 9, and he always says I have "a scientist's brain". I practised all week, and when I said it this afternoon my voice cracked anyway. I was sure he'd look disappointed, or worse, go quiet. He did go quiet for a bit. Then he said, "I would have chosen otherwise, Ritika. But you've clearly thought about it, and I trust your reasons." I nearly cried in the staffroom corridor. Uday was waiting outside and asked why I looked like I'd won a match. I said it felt like Sir had just started treating me as an equal. I still want to show him my economics projects. That's allowed, right?

qa.q: Which stream is Ritika taking?
qa.a: Commerce, not science.

qa.q: What was Ritika afraid of before telling Pankaj Sir?
qa.a: Ritika was nervous and afraid of disappointing Sir, after years of extra physics problems and talk of a scientist's brain.

qa.q: What did Pankaj Sir's reply do for the mentoring bond?
qa.a: By admitting he would choose differently but trusting Ritika's reasons, he made the relationship more equal instead of controlling.

qa.q: What might Pankaj Sir have felt during his quiet moment?
qa.a: He may have felt a pang of disappointment at losing a science student, then chosen respect for Ritika's own judgement.

grounding: Shows a student choosing a different stream than a mentor advised, fearing disappointment, and a mentor who trusts the student's reasons.

subtype: Stage 6: Boundaries and a lasting thread [Response]
passage: Clara had been in Ms Noa Visser's robotics club in Utrecht for three years, and now she was leaving for university. On the last day, Ms Visser gave her a printed list, "People to ask for help at uni", plus her school email. "Write whenever you like. I'll copy your mum in, same as always." Clara laughed. That had always been Ms Visser's way: meetings in the open lab with the door propped, messages through the club group, never private chats. Once, in Year 9, she had told the whole club, "If any adult, including me, ever asks you to keep a secret, gives you special gifts, or messages you privately outside club, tell a parent or another teacher. That's not telling tales. That's staying safe." Clara hugged her goodbye in front of everyone, her dad jingling the car keys, and knew the thread would hold.

qa.q: Where did Ms Visser hold meetings?
qa.a: In the open lab with the door propped.

qa.q: How did Clara feel on the last day with Ms Visser?
qa.a: Clara felt grateful and secure, laughing at the familiar rule and trusting that the thread between them would hold.

qa.q: Which of Ms Visser's habits kept the mentoring safe?
qa.a: Meeting in the open, using the club group instead of private chats, copying Clara's mum on emails, and teaching students to tell a parent if any adult asks for secrecy, gifts or private contact.

qa.q: How might Clara's dad see this mentor?
qa.a: Clara's dad probably feels reassured and trusting, since everything has been open and parents have always been included.

grounding: Shows a mentor keeping the relationship professional and open, and teaching that any adult asking for secrecy, gifts or private contact should be reported to a parent.

passage:
Monday, 9 p.m.
Did something brave today, or maybe silly. I asked Tarun from the analytics team whether he'd have coffee with me this week. He has been here eight years, and everyone goes to him when a project is stuck. I've been here seven months and still don't know whether to stay in reporting or push to move to product. I typed the message four times: "Hi Tarun, I'm Madhuri from reporting. Would you have 20 minutes this week? I'd love your advice on career paths." He replied in ten minutes: "Sure! Thursday 4 pm, the café downstairs?" I actually did a little dance by the printer. What I really want to ask isn't only which team. It's whether he thinks I'm good enough to go further. I don't know if I'll dare to say that part.

qa.q: When and where will Madhuri meet Tarun?
qa.a: Thursday at 4 pm, at the café downstairs.

qa.q: What does Madhuri most want from the coffee with Tarun?
qa.a: Madhuri feels unsure and hopeful, wanting practical advice about teams but even more a sign that someone experienced believes in Madhuri.

qa.q: What could help Madhuri get the most from Thursday's coffee?
qa.a: Writing down a few specific questions, and daring to ask honestly what strengths Tarun sees.

qa.q: How might Tarun see the invitation?
qa.a: Tarun seems happy to help, replying quickly and warmly, perhaps pleased to be asked.

grounding: Shows a junior employee unsure of the path ahead asking a senior colleague for coffee, wanting both practical answers and belief.

passage:
Wednesday night
Coffee with Vijay today, our third. He's twenty-two, sharp, and so worried about looking stupid that he never asks anything in meetings. So I told him about my first year here: the client deck I sent with the wrong company's logo on every slide, and crying in the stairwell afterwards. His eyes went wide. "You?" I also told him, honestly, that Ramesh in finance says yes in meetings and no over email, and that it's not personal. Vijay laughed properly for the first time. Then he admitted he had been stuck on the vendor report for a week and was scared to say so. That's the first real thing he's told me. I think sharing my disasters did more than any advice. Note to self, Tenzin: keep being honest, and keep the gossip kind.

qa.q: What mistake was in Tenzin's client deck in the first year?
qa.a: The wrong company's logo was on every slide.

qa.q: Why did Tenzin choose to share the stairwell story?
qa.a: Tenzin wanted Vijay to feel less alone and less afraid of looking stupid, and was glad when it helped him open up.

qa.q: What does this stage show about how rapport is built?
qa.a: Honest stories of struggle, plus a few frank tips about how people behave at work, made Vijay candid enough to admit he was stuck.

qa.q: What is it like for Vijay to hear that Tenzin once cried in the stairwell?
qa.a: Vijay is surprised and relieved, laughing properly for the first time and feeling safe enough to confess about the vendor report.

grounding: Shows a senior colleague sharing early failures and honest details of office politics, which helps a junior feel less alone and more candid.

passage: Bhavna, sit, and I'll tell you what my old boss Mrs Pinto told me when I was twenty-five. I, Gargi, was the quiet one on the team, and proud of it. I thought I was being thoughtful. One evening she called me in and said, "You speak too little in meetings." Then she gave examples. "On Monday you had the right numbers and let Suresh present the wrong ones. On Thursday the client asked about delays and you looked at your notebook." My ears went hot. I wanted to say, "I'm just not a show-off." I had the sentence ready. Instead I went home, sat on the balcony and made two lists: what she said that was unfair, and what was true. The second list was longer. That is the choice, Bhavna: defend yourself, or take what is useful.

qa.q: What did Gargi do when the client asked about delays?
qa.a: Gargi looked at the notebook.

qa.q: What was the young Gargi feeling when her ears went hot?
qa.a: She felt stung and defensive, with a ready answer that she was just not a show-off.

qa.q: What choice did Gargi make on the balcony, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Instead of defending herself, she listed what was unfair and what was true, and found the true list longer, which let her use the feedback.

qa.q: What might Mrs Pinto have been hoping for when she gave examples?
qa.a: She probably believed in Gargi and hoped that specific examples would make the feedback useful rather than simply hurtful.

grounding: Shows a mentor giving direct, specific feedback about speaking too little in meetings, and the mentee choosing to absorb what is useful rather than defend.

subtype: Stage 4: The mentee outgrows some advice [Receiver]
passage:
Sunday
On Friday Kalyani Ma'am told me again to stay off online platforms and let my portfolio speak "the old way": a printed book, agency visits, patience. Ten years ago that's how she got her first big client, and I love that story. But nearly every studio I've spoken to this year found its designers through their online work. I didn't say anything. I nodded, like always.
Tonight I feel torn. She's the reason I'm a designer at all; she spent Saturdays reviewing my sketches when nobody else would. Disagreeing feels almost like betrayal. But following advice I don't believe in isn't loyalty either.
I'm going to say it on Tuesday, carefully: "Ma'am, I think the industry has changed here. Can I show you what I'm seeing?" If she's the person I think she is, she'll listen.
Rajni

qa.q: How did Kalyani Ma'am get her first big client?
qa.a: Ten years ago, the old way: a printed book, agency visits and patience.

qa.q: Why does Rajni feel torn tonight?
qa.a: Rajni feels loyal and grateful to Kalyani Ma'am but doubtful about the advice, so disagreeing feels almost like betrayal.

qa.q: Is Rajni's plan for Tuesday a wise one, and why?
qa.a: Yes; asking respectfully to show what the studios are doing lets Rajni disagree with evidence while honouring the relationship.

qa.q: What might Kalyani Ma'am need to bring to Tuesday's talk?
qa.a: She may need the humility to hear that her ten-year-old path has changed, and to feel proud rather than hurt that Rajni is thinking independently.

grounding: Shows a mentee who feels loyal but doubtful about a mentor's outdated advice preparing to disagree respectfully.

passage: Deepa, you want to know about jealousy at work? Let your Ira Maasi confess one. At twenty-six I was a team lead, and I had trained Naveen from his first week: how to write specs, how to handle angry clients. Two years later he won the company's innovation award, the one I had wanted for myself for years. When they called his name, I clapped, and something small and sour turned in my chest. For a whole evening I told myself he had been lucky. Then I remembered his first spec, covered in my red pen, and the night he stayed late to fix it without complaint. The next morning I went to his desk and said, "Your win is partly my work too, and I'm proud of both of us." He grinned and said, "Mostly yours." That's when I learned that the best thing a mentor can feel is less needed.

qa.q: What award did Naveen win?
qa.a: The company's innovation award.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling when Naveen's name was called?
qa.a: She felt a small, sour pang of jealousy and hurt while clapping, having wanted that award for years.

qa.q: What turning point did Ira reach the next morning?
qa.a: She chose pride over rivalry, going to Naveen's desk to say his win was partly her work and that she was proud of both of them.

qa.q: How might Naveen have felt when Ira came to his desk?
qa.a: Naveen was likely touched and grateful, grinning and giving her credit with 'Mostly yours.'

grounding: Shows a mentor feeling a pang of hurt when a mentee's success passes her own, then choosing pride over rivalry.

subtype: Stage 6: Peer and paying it forward [Response]
passage: Harsha and I had dinner last Friday, and for the first time I noticed that I paid my own share without either of us thinking about it. Four years ago she was my senior at the lab, the one who taught me to label every sample twice and not to cry when an experiment failed. Now we argue about novels, and she asks my opinion on her research proposals. Somewhere along the way we became friends. Then on Monday a new junior, Ankur, stood at my bench looking lost, holding a pipette as if it might bite. I heard myself say, "Label everything twice. And come to me when it fails, not if." That evening I messaged Harsha: "Just said your line to someone new. Thank you, for all of it." She wrote back, "That's the whole point, Reena."

qa.q: What did Harsha teach about samples?
qa.a: To label every sample twice.

qa.q: How did Reena feel sending the message to Harsha?
qa.a: Reena felt grateful and warm, moved to realise that Harsha's help was now being passed on.

qa.q: How does Reena's action show the circle continuing?
qa.a: Reena guides Ankur with Harsha's own advice and thanks Harsha, showing gratitude by passing on the help received.

qa.q: What might Ankur be experiencing at Reena's bench?
qa.a: Ankur seems lost and nervous, and is probably relieved to hear a senior invite him to come for help when things fail.

grounding: Shows a mentoring bond becoming a friendship of equals, and the former mentee starting to guide someone newer out of gratitude.

passage: In Jorhat, at the tea stall outside his father's hardware shop, Kiran sketched the evening crowd on the back of a bill book. His father came out, glanced at it and said, "Your cousin Pritam cleared his bank exam. And you draw tea glasses." He went back inside. Kiran closed the book slowly. It was the same sentence in a hundred shapes. At ten: "Look at Pritam's marks." At fifteen, when he won the district art prize: "Prizes don't feed families." Now, at twenty, he had stopped showing anyone. His friend Tanvir, sipping tea beside him, said, "Your drawing is good, you know." Kiran shrugged. Inside, an old belief had set hard: whatever he became, it would never be enough for Baba.

qa.q: What had Pritam cleared?
qa.a: His bank exam.

qa.q: How does Kiran feel after years of these comments?
qa.a: Kiran feels hurt and hopeless, believing that nothing he becomes will ever be enough for Baba.

qa.q: What small step could Kiran take at this stage, before the hurt becomes a break?
qa.a: He could tell Baba calmly, perhaps with help from Tanvir or a trusted elder, how the comparisons feel, instead of silently giving up.

qa.q: What might Baba believe he is doing with these comparisons?
qa.a: Baba may think he is pushing Kiran towards security and a steady job, without seeing how much the dismissals wound him.

grounding: Shows a young man whose father has long compared him with a cousin and dismissed his art, building a belief that he can never be accepted.

passage:
Friday. The argument over Suraj's switch from engineering to music ended with his father shouting, "Then don't expect anything from this house!" Suraj packed a bag that night. At the door he said, "Don't call me. I mean it." His mother was crying in the kitchen.
Monday. He slept on a mattress in Abhinav's rented room and woke lighter than he had felt in years: nobody checking his marks, nobody sighing. Then his phone lit up with "Amma", and he turned it face down, his stomach dropping.
Two weeks later. Abhinav asked, "Will you go back?" Suraj said, "Never," too quickly. At night he lay awake, terrified of rent, of silence, of his mother's face. But going back meant admitting Papa was right, and pride held the door shut.

qa.q: Where did Suraj sleep after leaving home?
qa.a: On a mattress in Abhinav's rented room.

qa.q: What was Suraj feeling on Monday morning?
qa.a: He felt relieved and lighter, free of checks and sighs, yet his stomach dropped when Amma called.

qa.q: What small step could keep a door open at this stage without giving up his choice?
qa.a: Suraj could send Amma a short message that he is safe, keeping a thread alive even while he needs distance.

qa.q: What might Amma be going through as her calls go unanswered?
qa.a: Amma is likely worried and grieving, caught between her son and her husband and left without news.

grounding: Shows a young man moving out after a harsh argument over his course, relieved and terrified at once, with pride making the break feel final.
